Pay Yourself First: The Simple Habit That Builds Real Wealth

It's one of the oldest rules in personal finance — and one of the most ignored

Ethan Marchand·August 13, 2026·6 min read

Of everything I talk about with clients, "pay yourself first" is the least sophisticated idea in the room — and it's also the one that predicts long-term financial outcomes better than almost anything else. The concept isn't new; it's been around for close to a century. What's changed is how easy it's become to actually do it, and how rarely people take advantage of that.

The idea, in one sentence

Before you pay a single bill or spend a single discretionary dollar, a portion of every paycheque gets moved into savings and investments — treated as a fixed obligation, not a nice-to-have. Whatever's left after that is what you actually live on. It's the exact opposite of the way most households handle money, which is to pay everything else first and save whatever happens to be left over at the end of the month. For the vast majority of people, "whatever's left over" rounds to zero.

Why the order matters so much

This isn't really a math problem — it's a behaviour problem, and paying yourself first is a behavioural fix. Spending naturally expands to fill whatever's available; that's not a character flaw, it's just how budgets work in practice for almost everyone. If saving is the last thing that happens each month, it competes with every other want and need in your life and loses more often than it wins. If saving is the first thing that happens — ideally automatically, on payday, before you ever see the money — it stops being a decision you have to make every single month. It just happens.

Key takeaway

You don't need willpower if the money is already gone before you can spend it. Automate the transfer on payday and the habit takes care of itself.

How to actually set it up

There's no universal percentage that's right for everyone — someone carrying high-interest debt has a different starting point than someone with none. What matters more than the exact number is starting with something and automating it, then increasing it as your income grows rather than letting your lifestyle absorb every raise.

  • Set up an automatic transfer for the same day your pay lands — not a manual transfer you have to remember to make.
  • Start with an amount you genuinely won't miss, then raise it every time your income does — a percentage of a raise is far less painful to redirect than a percentage of your current take-home pay.
  • Send it somewhere with a real purpose — an emergency fund first if you don't have one, then a TFSA or RRSP for the long term, not a chequing account it can quietly leak back out of.
  • Treat it exactly like rent or a loan payment in your own head — non-negotiable, not the thing that flexes when the month gets tight.

It applies at the corporate level too

If you're an incorporated business owner, the exact same principle applies one level up, and it's just as easy to skip. It's common for surplus cash to sit in a corporation indefinitely — not reinvested in the business, not paid out, just accumulating with no real plan attached to it. "Pay yourself first" as a business owner means deciding, deliberately and on a schedule, how much of that surplus gets moved into structured savings, investments, or insurance planning — rather than leaving it to accumulate as passive income the CRA will happily tax and that offers no real strategy behind it.

Where that money should actually go — a personal TFSA, a corporate investment account, an exempt life insurance policy funding future retirement income and the corporation's Capital Dividend Account — depends entirely on your situation. But the habit underneath all of it is the same one: decide the amount, automate the move, and build your spending around what's left rather than the other way around.
